title: Easy beats heroic
hookLine: the well-known willpower-drain effect failed a large 2016 replication (Hagger et al.)

cards: A lab in the late 1990s. A plate of warm chocolate chip cookies sits on a table, next to a bowl of radishes. Some hungry volunteers are allowed the cookies.
Others are told: radishes only, please. Then everyone gets an impossible puzzle. The radish group, who had spent their self-control resisting the cookies, gave up sooner.
The idea that grew from this was simple and everywhere: willpower is a tank of fuel, and every time you resist something, the tank runs lower. Hundreds of studies followed.
Then, in 2016, two dozen labs tried again, carefully, all at once.

teach.b: The 2016 project, led by Martin Hagger with labs across several countries, ran one agreed version of a classic willpower test, two tasks back to back rather than the cookies, on more than two thousand people.

The draining effect came out close to zero. Other researchers have argued about the method, and the debate isn't fully closed, but the neat picture of a willpower tank running dry is much shakier than the posters say.
Remember compared to what. If willpower isn't a tank, then struggling isn't proof that yours is small.
And several studies suggest that people who seem to have lots of self-control don't spend their days heroically resisting temptation. They meet fewer temptations.
They've set things up so the good thing is easy and the other thing is a little further away. Their habits do the work.
The Tao Te Ching, the Chinese classic, has a word for acting without forcing: wu wei. It came up with the swimmer at the falls, who went in with the whirl and came out with the swirl.
The book advises doing the hard thing while it's still easy, and the great thing while it's still small.
Epictetus said something close from the Stoic side: start with small things, a little spilled oil, a little stolen wine, and practice there.
Heroic plans feel wonderful at night and collapse by Thursday: an hour of meditation, every day, starting tomorrow.
Easy plans look almost silly: two minutes, the cue does the remembering, cushion already on the floor. Silly wins.
Make the practice so easy you'd feel odd skipping it.

how: People who keep a daily practice often make it small and set it up in advance, like leaving a cushion out or keeping the session to two minutes, rather than relying on willpower each day.

o: pushing through by sheer strength of will
keeping a strict schedule for every hour of the day
acting without forcing, letting things flow easily

games.q: willpower and ease — tap the pairs.

s: science has shown willpower is a tank that runs dry
a large 2016 replication across two dozen labs found close to no effect; the debate goes on.
people with strong self-control often just meet fewer temptations
several studies suggest they set things up so resisting is rarely needed.
the Tao Te Ching advises tackling hard things while they're easy
do the hard thing while it's easy, the great thing while it's small.

games.q: it's Sunday night and you're inspired. what plan is most likely to still be running next Sunday?
o: an hour of meditation every day, starting tomorrow.
two minutes after the kettle, cushion already out.
wait until you feel more disciplined.
games.why: the easy plan wins. make the practice so small and so ready that skipping it would feel odd.

practice: Take the practice you tied to your cue yesterday and make it easier: shorter, maybe one minute instead of five; closer, with the cushion or chair where you'll trip over it; or fewer steps, with the note on the kettle itself.
Pick the one change that removes one bit of friction. Then sit, and notice how it feels to plan without clenching.

wordCard.voice: Wu wei, acting without forcing: don't rely on a willpower tank, make the good thing easy and let habit carry it.

orig.note: Chinese: literally not-doing; action without forcing, a key idea of the Tao Te Ching.

carryVoice: Your line: start with small things. A chair already set out is a practice half done. See you tomorrow.
